query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The superconducting state in the selected high-entropy alloy emerges through conventional BCS electron–phonon pairing that is modulated by the degree of atomic disorder (i.e. high configurational entropy) in its simple lattice. Higher configurational disorder enhances the effective electron–phonon coupling in the dirty limit, favoring an isotropic s‐wave gap and robust superconductivity at low temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy initially synthesized with a simple crystalline structure (e.g., BCC) and high configurational disorder due to random mixing of five or more elements.
generation.intervention: Prepare a controlled variant of the alloy with reduced configurational disorder (i.e. fewer elements or more ordered mixing) while keeping the crystal structure similar.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature regime (below ~10 K) under ambient pressure (or moderate pressures) where superconductivity can be observed and characterized.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic arrangements and site-to-site variations (i.e. local chemical disorder) which can be quantified by techniques such as X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, as well as via spectroscopic measurements of the density-of-states at the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy creates significant atomic-scale disorder that broadens the phonon spectrum and modifies the density-of-states, thereby tuning the electron–phonon coupling strength. In the dirty limit (due to disorder scattering), this produces a conventional isotropic s-wave superconducting state as described by BCS theory, which is robust against variations in pressure and temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-entropy alloy will exhibit superconductivity with a transition temperature and critical fields (both lower and upper) consistent with dirty-limit s-wave BCS behavior. The variant with reduced configurational disorder is expected to show altered (likely lower or differently tuned) Tc and critical fields, indicating the role of disorder in controlling the superconducting parameters.
generation.baseline: The superconducting behavior (Tc, Hc1, Hc2) observed in the original, highly disordered high-entropy alloy sample.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for alloys with a simple (e.g., BCC) lattice and sufficiently high mixing entropy. It may not apply for alloys with drastically different crystal structures or cases where other interactions (such as magnetism or strong electronic correlations) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the effect (i.e. precise changes in Tc and critical fields) depends on the specifics of the alloy composition and the nature of the disorder. Direct quantification of electron–phonon coupling modifications and the density-of-states requires further experimental and computational studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: (a) the target high-entropy alloy with high configurational disorder and (b) a comparison alloy with similar overall composition but intentionally reduced disorder (e.g., by limiting the number of elements or inducing chemical ordering). Measure the superconducting transition temperature (Tc), lower and upper critical fields (Hc1 and Hc2), and perform tunneling or penetration-depth measurements to probe the superconducting gap symmetry.
measurements: Resistance vs. temperature to determine Tc
Magnetization and susceptibility to measure Hc1 and Hc2
Scanning tunneling spectroscopy or penetration depth measurements to confirm isotropic s-wave pairing
Structural characterization (XRD, TEM) to quantify the degree of chemical disorder
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the configurational disorder in the comparison sample does not lead to a statistically significant change in the superconducting transition temperature, critical fields, or gap symmetry compared to the highly disordered alloy, then the hypothesis that superconductivity is primarily governed by disorder-modulated electron–phonon coupling would be undermined.

Enhanced Superconducting Critical Parameters in a New High-Entropy Alloy Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08

Abstract: The structural and physical properties of the new titanium- and niobium-rich type-A high-entropy alloy (HEA) superconductor Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 (in at.%) were studied by X-ray powder diffraction, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, magnetization, electrical resistivity, and specific heat measurements. In addition, electronic structure calculations were performed using two complementary methods: the Korringa–Kohn–Rostoker Coherent Potential Approximation (KKR-CPA) and the Projector Augmented Wave (PAW) within Density Functional Theory (DFT). The results obtained indicate that the alloy exhibits type II superconductivity with a critical temperature close to 7.5 K, an intermediate electron–phonon coupling, and an upper critical field of 12.2(1) T. This finding indicates that Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 has one of the highest upper critical fields among all known HEA superconductors.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEA) form through the random arrangement of five or more chemical elements on a crystalline lattice. Despite the significant amount of resulting compositional disorder, a subset of HEAs enters a superconducting state below critical temperatures, Tc<10 K. The superconducting properties of the known HEAs seem to suffice a Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) description, but little is known about their superconducting order parameter and the microscopic role of disorder. We report on magnetic susceptibility measurements on films of the superconducting HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x for characterizing the lower and upper critical fields Hc,1(T) and Hc,2(T), respectively as a function of temperature T. Our resulting analysis of the Ginzburg–Landau coherence length and penetration depth demonstrates that HEAs of this type are single-band isotropic s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit.
